blocks.prompt: The Meerkat on Guard Duty
blocks.text: A meerkat is small enough to sit in your two hands. It lives in a big family in the dry sand of Africa. All day the family digs for bugs to eat. But a meerkat with its head down a hole cannot see the sky. So someone has to watch. One meerkat climbs onto a rock and stands up tall. This meerkat is the guard. It does not dig. It just looks. If a hawk comes, the guard barks a warning. Every meerkat drops its bug and runs for the nearest hole. When the sky is safe again, the guard barks a different sound, and the whole family comes back out to dig.

blocks.prompt: The Watcher on the Rock
blocks.text: The Kalahari is a huge stretch of red sand and dry grass in southern Africa. Nights there are cold. So when a meerkat family climbs out of its burrow in the morning, the first thing it does is sit up and face the sun. The fur on a meerkat's belly is thin, and the skin under it is dark. That dark skin soaks up heat, the way a black shirt does on a hot day. Once the family is warm, the digging starts. Almost everything a meerkat eats is buried. Beetles, grubs, spiders, and small lizards all hide under the sand, so a meerkat has to shove its face into the ground and dig with its long front claws. That works, but it creates a problem. A meerkat with its head in a hole cannot see an eagle. So the family shares the job of watching. One meerkat stops eating, climbs onto a rock or a low branch, stands up on its back legs, and props itself on its tail. While it is on duty it makes a soft, steady call. That call means one thing: I am watching, keep digging. If the soft call stops, every meerkat looks up.

blocks.prompt: The Scorpion Lesson
blocks.text: A scorpion is a difficult meal. It has claws at the front, a stinger at the back, and it fights. A grown meerkat handles one with practiced calm: it darts in, snaps the stinger off the tail, and eats the rest. A meerkat is also partly resistant to scorpion venom, so a sting that would put a person in a hospital is survivable for a two-pound animal in the Kalahari. But a meerkat pup does not know any of that. It is born underground and comes out at about three weeks old with no idea what a scorpion even is. So the adults teach it, and they teach it in stages. When a pup is very young, an adult kills a scorpion first, then hands over the dead body. There is nothing to fear and nothing to learn except the taste. As the pup gets a little older, the adults change the lesson. Now they bring a live scorpion with the stinger bitten off. It scuttles, the pup chases, and if the pup fumbles it, an adult nudges the scorpion back within reach. Only when the pup is nearly grown do the adults hand over a whole live scorpion and step back. How do the adults know which stage a pup is ready for? They listen. Pups beg with a call, and the call changes as they grow. Researchers played recordings of older pups' begging calls next to young pups, and the adults brought live prey to babies who were far too small for it. The adults were not counting weeks. They were going by the sound.

5.title: The Meerkat on Guard Duty
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Suricata suricatta, a mongoose of the Kalahari
A mob runs from about 3 to 50 members
Alarm calls carry both the type of danger and how urgent it is
Dark eye patches work like built-in sunglasses
Non-retractable claws built for digging, not gripping

blocks.prompt: A Language of Warnings
blocks.text: Most animal alarm calls say very little. They say danger, and they say it loudly, and every animal in earshot does the same thing: it runs. A meerkat's alarm calls are stranger and more useful than that, because a meerkat does not have one escape plan. It has several, and picking the wrong one can kill it. Consider the problem. If a martial eagle is dropping out of the sky, the only safe place is underground, and you have seconds. If a jackal is crossing the plain half a mile off, diving into a hole is a waste of a good morning, because the jackal is slow, visible, and probably not hunting yet. If a snake is coiled in the grass three feet from the pups, running underground is the worst possible move, because underground is exactly where the snake is heading. Three dangers, three different correct answers. So the meerkat's warning has to carry more than the word danger. Researchers who recorded thousands of these calls in the Kalahari found that each one encodes two separate pieces of information at once. The first is what kind of predator it is: a bird in the air, a mammal on the ground, or a snake. The second is how urgent the situation is, coded in the roughness and pitch of the sound. A low-urgency bird call and a high-urgency bird call are recognizably related, the way a murmur and a shout are the same word said two ways. Play a high-urgency aerial alarm from a hidden speaker and the whole mob flattens itself and bolts for a bolt-hole. Play the low-urgency version and the meerkats simply stand, scan the sky, and go back to digging. Play the snake alarm and they do something else entirely: they gather, they approach, and they mob the danger together rather than run from it. The meerkats are not just hearing an alert. They are hearing a description, and they are choosing their response from it. That is a small thing to say about a two-pound animal, and it is also not a small thing at all.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Suricata suricatta, a cooperative mongoose
Sentinel duty is taken in turns, usually after feeding
Alarm calls encode predator type and urgency together
Pups are taught with dead, then disabled, then live prey
Adults judge the lesson by the pup's begging call

blocks.prompt: The Selfish Sentinel: What the Meerkat Actually Owes Its Family
blocks.text: For decades the meerkat on the rock was biology's favorite little hero. Here was an animal that gave up its own breakfast, climbed to the most exposed spot on the plain, made itself the most visible thing for a hundred yards in any direction, and screamed a warning that saved everyone but itself. It was cooperation you could photograph. It appeared in documentaries and textbooks as a clean example of an animal paying a personal cost for the good of the group. Then researchers in the Kalahari did something unglamorous. They watched, and they wrote down what actually happened, and the story fell apart in an interesting way. The first finding was about timing. A meerkat did not take a turn on guard at random, and it did not take one while hungry. It took one after it had eaten well. Guarding, it turned out, was what a full meerkat did with its afternoon. The second finding was worse for the hero story. The sentinel was not in more danger than the foragers. It was in less. The sentinel is the animal with its head up and its eyes on the sky. It sees the eagle first. It is also, almost always, the animal standing closest to a bolt-hole, because that is where it chose to stand. When the alarm goes up, the sentinel is not sacrificing itself to buy the others time. It is already halfway home. Researchers gave this the deliberately unromantic name of the selfish sentinel: guarding may simply be the safest available job for a meerkat that no longer needs to eat, and the warning bark may be a side effect of doing it. This is not a story about meerkats being frauds. It is a story about how easy it is to see nobility in a behavior when nobility is the thing you went looking for. And the deflation is not the end of it. The same population produced a finding that is harder to explain away. Adult meerkats teach. They hand young pups dead scorpions, then live scorpions with the stinger removed, then whole live ones, escalating the difficulty as the pup grows. Teaching is rare in animals and expensive to fake, because the adult loses a meal, spends time, and gains nothing immediate. When researchers played recordings of older pups' begging calls beside pups too young for the lesson, the adults upgraded the prey anyway. They were reading a signal and adjusting their instruction to it. So the meerkat is not the hero of the documentary and not the cynic of the correction. It is an animal that will take the safest job available and call it guard duty, and will also lose its own dinner, repeatedly, to walk a pup through a lesson it cannot yet survive on its own. Both are true. The uncomfortable part is not that the sentinel turned out to be selfish. It is that we never needed the sentinel to be a hero. We needed to look.
